name: Avon Curve
description:
Before the incorporation, Avondale was gentrifying so fast the displacement was visible in real time — craft breweries and farm-to-table restaurants colonizing blocks where working-class Polish and Latino families had lived for generations. When the corps came, the gentrification didn't stop. It metastasized. Vantage Meridian's lifestyle subsidiary — a brand called CurveLiving — purchased the entire Kennedy Expressway frontage and converted it into a Tier 3-4 residential and commercial development marketed as 'authentic urban living.' The marketing materials featured the old brewery buildings. They did not feature the people who had been evicted from them.

Avon Curve is the Meridian Core's outer edge — the place where corporate territory thins from sovereign to 'brand-managed' to 'influenced' to nothing, all within a fifteen-minute walk. The CurveLiving development occupies the district's western spine: renovated industrial buildings filled with neural-interface-optimized apartments, curated food halls, and the kind of coffee shops where the barista's augments cost more than a Shelf resident's annual income. It is beautiful, expensive, and haunted by the ghost of every community it displaced. The craft breweries are still here — now corporate-owned, producing algorithmically optimized IPAs that taste like data sets instead of beer.

East of the CurveLiving spine, the district degrades rapidly into what the residents call the Backslide — blocks where the corporate development ran out of budget or interest and the original neighborhood infrastructure was left half-demolished. The Backslide is a patchwork of gutted buildings, improvised housing, and the kind of small businesses that exist because someone needed them to, not because a market analysis justified them. The contrast between the CurveLiving spine and the Backslide is GLMZ's most visible demonstration of how corporate development works: invest in the front, abandon the back, and put a wall between them.

Kyle has a contact in the Backslide — a former CurveLiving construction worker who was injured on the job, denied corporate medical coverage, and now runs an unlicensed augment clinic from a gutted brewery that still smells like hops. The clinic is good. The beer the guy makes on the side is better.

sights: CurveLiving's renovated industrial buildings — exposed brick, smart glass, corporate pastoral
The Backslide's gutted blocks visible two streets away from the development's edge
Craft brewery signage — both the corporate versions and the illegal ones in the Backslide
The wall between CurveLiving and the Backslide — not a literal wall, but a change in lighting, maintenance, and reality
Food halls with holographic menus next to blocks where people cook on salvaged camp stoves
The old Kennedy Expressway infrastructure repurposed as CurveLiving's elevated promenade
sounds: The CurveLiving side: curated ambient music, clinking glasses, the murmur of comfortable conversation
The Backslide: construction, argument, the sound of people building lives from scraps
The maglev line that replaced the Kennedy Expressway — a constant presence overhead
Brewing equipment — both the corporate precision of CurveLiving's operations and the improvised clatter of Backslide batches
smells: Hops and malt — the one constant across both halves of the district
CurveLiving's curated food hall aromas — designed to attract, not nourish
The Backslide's cooking: honest food made with whatever's available
Industrial dust from the half-demolished blocks where development stopped mid-swing
atmosphere.feel: Vertigo. Walking from CurveLiving into the Backslide takes three minutes and feels like falling through the tier system in real time. The Curve is the city's most efficient empathy generator for anyone paying attention, and the most efficient empathy suppressant for anyone who isn't. The corporate side is comfortable. The Backslide is real. The distance between them is the width of a street.

demographics: CurveLiving: approximately 20,000 Tier 3-4 residents. Backslide: approximately 35,000 Tier 1-2 residents, ethnically mixed with significant Polish and Latino legacy communities. The two populations share a district name and a mutual resentment that manifests as studied avoidance.
dangers: The CurveLiving security perimeter — crossing from the Backslide triggers profiling algorithms
The Backslide's structural instability — half-demolished buildings are not half-safe buildings
Gentrification pressure — CurveLiving expands by a block every few years, displacing Backslide residents
The social toxicity of living next to wealth you cannot access
Corporate security treating Backslide residents as threats by default
opportunities: The Backslide's unlicensed services — augment clinics, repair shops, real food
CurveLiving as a hunting ground for corporate intelligence and credentials
The district's split personality as cover — move between worlds in three minutes
Backslide brewing culture — unlicensed beer as currency and social lubricant
Former CurveLiving workers with insider knowledge of corporate construction and security systems
story_hooks: CurveLiving is expanding again, and the Backslide community has hired Kyle to make the developer's survey team reconsider their timeline
A CurveLiving resident has discovered that their 'authentic industrial loft' was built on top of a sealed community archive containing pre-incorporation property records
Kyle's augment clinic contact in the Backslide has been offered a corporate buyout that smells like a trap
frequented_by: CurveLiving tenants who never cross into the Backslide
Backslide residents who cross into CurveLiving for work and are invisible while they do it
Operators using the district transition as a vanishing technique
Craft beer enthusiasts who know the Backslide brews are better
Corporate scouts from Vantage Meridian's expansion division
